speaker_notes.note: This student example about Clinton and one-time versus repeated infidelity is heavily ASR-degraded, but it appears to be arguing that a single mistake differs from a sustained sexual relationship.

interactions.summary: Students keep answering Jiang's demand for a concrete redemptive act by shifting from instant absolution toward long-term character change and regained trust.
Jiang halts the repair talk and asks a deeper question about why cheating is bad at all, drawing out answers about remorse, relationship versus mistake, and the seriousness of covenantal violation.

claims.claim: A student argues that human relationships differ from divine judgment because trust can be rebuilt only over time through visible change of character rather than by undoing the past.
Jiang refuses to leave the issue at apology or future self-improvement and instead asks the class to define what cheating actually damages and why it matters.
One student seems to distinguish a one-time mistake from an ongoing affair, suggesting that repeated involvement changes the moral status more than a single lapse does.
Another student says that part of redemption would require the betrayed partner to see genuine remorse, since a person can cheat without actually caring about the wrong.

signature_moments.moment: The class lands on a hard limit: you cannot uncheat, so the only imaginable repair is becoming a different person over time.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can't go back in time and uncheat
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It gives the classroom its clearest practical account of why betrayal cannot be repaired by a single compensating act.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips the discussion down to the primitive question beneath all repair talk: why is cheating bad in the first place, and who cares?
signature_moments.source_phrase: Why is cheating a bad thing? Like who cares?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the method turn that moves the lecture from social convention to first-principles analysis of vow and trust.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The relational good students keep returning to: once damaged by betrayal, it can only be regained through time, character change, and credible future conduct.
A proposed sign that the betrayer understands the wrong, rather than merely wanting the consequences to disappear.

chronology_notes.note: The class shifts from asking how redemption could happen to asking what cheating destroys, with human trust, character, and remorse emerging as the first concrete answers.

uncertainty_notes.note: The Clinton example is semantically noisy enough that only the broad contrast between one-off mistake and continuing affair is stable.
